newsitem.title: UK: UK securities official urges check of Labour plan.
newsitem.headline: UK securities official urges check of Labour plan.

text.p: A full analysis should be carried out before any major changes are made to Britain's financial regulatory framework, as proposed by the opposition Labour Party, a City watchdog official said on Tuesday.
"I'm not convinced a full analysis has been done on the issues," said Richard Farrant, chief executive at the Securities and Futures Authority (SFA) in London.
Speaking at a conference here, he said these were his views, not necessarily those of the SFA.

Farrant said the proposals would mean considerable transition costs at a time when watchdogs are focused on more important issues such as the extremely competitive business climate in the London financial community.

Alistair Darling, Labour's spokesman on City matters, has said Labour would streamline the regulatory bodies in London, giving the Securities Investment Board (SIB) greater responsibility, particularly for regulation.

Currently Britain's regulatory framework includes the SFA, the SIB, investment watchdog IMRO (the Investment Management Regulatory Organisation) and the Serious Fraud Office, as well as the Bank of England.

Ferrant told the conference the SFA was constantly reviewing its procedures and regulations to help firms manage risk. He said he would prefer firms be put more in charge of their own rules and regulations and that rules should contain less detail.
He added the SFA tries to reward companies for coming up with their own policies that can be put into action.
He said it was important that capital requirements be made separate from risk management. "Capital is no substitute for risk management," he said.
He cited Barings as an example.
"Everybody thought they had ample capital until they discovered they didn't have any. When it comes to the crunch capital is no good at all."
Self regulation encourages innovative risk control, permits a holistic approach, permits more accuracy, and allows firms to learn by their mistakes, he said.
